ety.text: PIE word *h₁óynos Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ís? Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos Proto-Germanic *ainaz Proto-West Germanic *ain Old English ān Middle English on English one From Middle English oon, on, oan, an, from Old English ān (“one”), from Proto-West Germanic *ain, from Proto-Germanic *ainaz (“one”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos (“single, one”). Doublet of a, an, and Uno.

Analogous to several senses of Hokkien 個／个 (ê) and Mandarin 的 (de, declarative particle, nominalizer, etc.). This semantic loan might have stemmed from the apparent similarity between one as a prop-word and 的 (de) or 個 /个 (ê) as a nominalizer (e.g. 青色的 (“the green one”)). Compare Cantonese 嘅 (ge³).

senses.d: The number represented by the Arabic numeral 1; the numerical value equal to that cardinal number.
ex: In some religions, there is more than one god.
In many cultures, a baby turns one year old a year after its birth.

senses.d: The first positive number in the set of natural numbers.
The cardinality of the smallest nonempty set.
The ordinality of an element which has no predecessor, usually called first or number one.
One thing (among a group of others); one member of a group.
ex: Any one of the boys.
Every one of the bank’s employees.

senses.d: The first mentioned of two things or people, as opposed to the other.
ex: She offered him an apple and an orange; he took (the) one and left the other.
I am one of the few women who've climbed Everest.

senses.d: Any person (applying to people in general).
ex: One’s guilt may trouble one, but it is best not to let oneself be troubled by things which cannot be changed.  One shouldn’t be too quick to judge.
My neighbor talks to one like a teacher.

senses.d: Any person, entity or thing.
ex: "driver", noun: one who drives.

senses.d: The digit or figure 1.
A one-dollar bill.
ex: I need some ones to make change.

senses.d: One o'clock, either a.m. or p.m.
ex: The ophthalmic surgeon attends Tuesdays and Saturdays, at half-past one.

senses.d: One run scored by hitting the ball and running between the wickets; a single.
A joke or amusing anecdote.
ex: Did you hear the one about the agnostic dyslexic insomniac?

senses.d: A question.
ex: You already know, so you can answer that one yourselves

senses.d: An alcoholic drink, especially a pint or can of beer.
ex: I had a quick one after work
There’s nothing better than drinking a cold one when the weather’s boiling outside

senses.d: An act of sexual intercourse.
ex: Just a quick one before work

senses.d: A person or thing (having some specified characteristic or attribute).
ex: Now, he's a curious one.
Well, well, well, it seems the silent one does have a voice, after all.

senses.d: A person with a tendency to do something.
ex: He's not one for pulling his punches.
Pause. They look meaningly at one another. / "You are a one for being roundabout," says the lady.

senses.d: Of a period of time, being particular.
ex: One day the prince set forth to kill the dragon that had brought terror to his father’s kingdom for centuries.

senses.d: Being a single, unspecified thing; a; any.
ex: My aunt used to say, "One day is just like the other."

senses.d: Sole, only.
ex: He is the one man who can help you.
The one male audience member at the concert is invited on stage.

senses.d: Whole, entire.
ex: Body and soul are not separate; they are one.

senses.d: In agreement.
ex: We are one on the importance of learning.

senses.d: The same.
ex: The two types look very different, but are one species.

senses.d: A single.
ex: There was one box of biscuits available.

senses.d: Being a preeminent example.
ex: He is one hell of a guy.

senses.d: Being an unknown person with the specified name; see also “a certain”.
ex: The town records from 1843 showed the overnight incarceration of one “A. Lincoln”.

senses.d: To cause to become one; to gather into a single whole; to unite.
ex: And both shall be oned in eternal happiness.
Knit and oned to God human beings are irrevocably in relationship with the divine.

senses.d: Used at the end of a sentence to highlight the characteristics of someone or something.
ex: Got almonds one.
How come so heavy one ah?

senses.d: Used at the end of a sentence to highlight the originator of something.
ex: My friend send one.
Who say one?

senses.d: Used at the end of a sentence to highlight the likelihood of something occurring, as a characteristic of something else.
ex: Can easily get lost one, know?

senses.d: A nominalizer used to form a noun phrase without a head noun.
ex: The sell fruits one go home already.

senses.d: Used as a relative pronoun at the end of a relative clause.
ex: The bird that make a lot of noise one is gone already.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French un, from Old French un, from Latin ūnum, accusative singular of ūnus (“one”), from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos.
Inherited from Latin ūnus, from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos.

Inherited from Old Spanish uno, from Latin ūnus (“one”), from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos (“one, single”). Cognates include Ancient Greek οἶος (oîos), French un, & Russian один (odin). Doublet of un.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ũu (“one; a”), from Latin ūnum (“one”), from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos (“one”). Doublet of uno.
Inherited from Old French une, from Latin ūna, feminine of ūnus.
